Proposed: (remove)
Reason: Certified reinsurers and reciprocal jurisdiction reinsurers are two separate categories under the NAIC Credit for Reinsurance Models #785/#786; they are not synonyms.

Proposed: Under NAIC Credit for Reinsurance Model Law #785 and Regulation #786, certified reinsurers from qualified jurisdictions post reduced collateral based on their rating. A separate category added in 2019, reciprocal jurisdiction reinsurers, can post no collateral.
Reason: Explains the distinction the current AKA gets wrong.

Current: A 2022 federal law protecting patients from surprise bills for most emergency care and some out-of-network care at in-network facilities.
Proposed: A federal law, signed in December 2020 and in effect since January 1, 2022, that protects patients from surprise bills for most emergency care and some out-of-network care at in-network facilities.
Reason: The Act was enacted December 27, 2020 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021; only its main protections took effect in 2022.

Current: An insurer below 200% RBC triggers regulator action.
Proposed: An insurer whose capital falls below 200% of its Authorized Control Level RBC must file a corrective plan with its regulator; stronger regulator action follows at lower levels.
Reason: 200% of ACL is the Company Action Level (the insurer must act); regulator-directed action starts at lower ratios (150%, 100%, 70%). Readers may also confuse 200% RBC with a percentage of the minimum.

Current: The starting age is set by federal law (currently 73, rising to 75 in 2033).
Proposed: The starting age is set by federal law (SECURE 2.0): 73 for people born 1951-1959, and 75 for people born in 1960 or later.
Reason: SECURE 2.0 sets age 75 for those who attain age 74 after Dec 31, 2032; the first age-75 RMDs occur in 2035, not 2033.

Current: US reinsurance is regulated through ceding insurers' credit-for-reinsurance rules.
Proposed: US reinsurers are licensed and supervised by their home state like other insurers; non-US reinsurers are regulated mainly indirectly, through the credit-for-reinsurance rules that apply to the ceding insurer.
Reason: Current note implies all reinsurance regulation is indirect; US-domiciled reinsurers are directly regulated for solvency.

Current: In the US it is applied strongly in marine insurance under federal maritime law; other lines follow state misrepresentation statutes.
Proposed: In the US it is applied in marine insurance as a rule of federal maritime law in most federal circuits (the Fifth Circuit applies state law instead); other lines follow state misrepresentation statutes.
Reason: The Fifth Circuit (Albany Ins. Co. v. Anh Thi Kieu, 1991) held the doctrine is not entrenched and applies state law; the note overstates uniformity.

Current: Exists in about 30 states and D.C.
Proposed: Exists in more than 30 states and D.C. (NAIC counts 33 states plus D.C.), and the number has been growing.
Reason: NAIC puts the count at 33 states plus D.C.; 'about 30' understates it.

Current: An insurer mails an annual privacy notice.
Proposed: An insurer gives a privacy notice when you become a customer; since 2015 an annual notice is needed only if it changes its practices or shares data in ways that require an opt-out.
Reason: The FAST Act (Dec 2015) removed the annual notice requirement under stated conditions; the example implies it is always required.

Proposed: Currently authorized through December 31, 2027 (2019 reauthorization); Congress was considering a further extension in 2026.
Reason: Accurate today, but the House passed a reauthorization (H.R. 7128) in June 2026 and a Senate bill is pending; the note will date quickly and should be checked before publishing.

Current: The Nonadmitted and Reinsurance Reform Act (NRRA, 2010) gives the insured's home state sole authority to tax.
Proposed: The Nonadmitted and Reinsurance Reform Act (NRRA, 2010) gives the insured's home state sole authority to regulate the placement and to collect the premium tax.
Reason: NRRA gives the home state authority over both regulation of the placement and premium tax, not just tax.

Current: Adopted through the NAIC Valuation Manual beginning 2017.
Proposed: Introduced through the NAIC Valuation Manual, effective January 1, 2017, with a three-year transition; required for new life business from 2020.
Reason: Adds the phase-in so readers don't assume PBR was mandatory in 2017.

Current: NAIC statutory reporting uses the term DCC.
Proposed: Since 1998 NAIC statutory reporting uses Defense and Cost Containment (DCC), which is close to but not identical to ALAE.
Reason: DCC and ALAE overlap but are not the same category; e.g., some outside adjuster fees are ALAE but fall under Adjusting and Other (AO).

Proposed: ULAE; roughly AO (Adjusting and Other) in NAIC reporting
Reason: AO also includes some claim-specific adjusting costs, so it is not an exact synonym for ULAE.

Proposed: (remove)
Reason: The Statement of Actuarial Opinion is the document the appointed actuary signs, not another name for the actuary; move it to Related Terms.

Current: A decision by the insurer not to offer coverage or not to pay a claim.
Proposed: A decision by the insurer not to offer or renew coverage for an applicant or risk.
Reason: In US usage 'declination' is an underwriting term; refusing to pay a claim is a claim denial.

Current: An auditor checks there's a 10% chance of a 10% loss.
Proposed: An auditor checks there's at least a 10% chance the reinsurer loses at least 10% of the premium (on a present-value basis).
Reason: The '10-10' rule measures the loss relative to the reinsurance premium; the current example leaves the base undefined.

Current: Lloyd's underwriters stamp the slip for their lines.
Proposed: Lloyd's underwriters sign the slip for their lines; today this is usually an electronic Market Reform Contract (MRC).
Reason: Modern London placements use the MRC and electronic placing; the paper slip wording is dated.

Current: An ACA rule requiring employers with 50 or more full-time employees to offer affordable coverage or pay a penalty.
Proposed: An ACA rule requiring employers with 50 or more full-time employees (including full-time equivalents) to offer affordable coverage or pay a penalty.
Reason: Part-time hours count toward the 50 threshold via full-time equivalents.

Proposed: Medium
Reason: Premium tax is paid by insurers and rarely seen by consumers or used in daily learner contexts; High overstates it compared with terms like Deductible.
